opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's one of the most frustrating misreadings of my work. I don't hate AI. I've wanted AI to work since I was a kid; I wrote my first programs as a teenager trying to get machines to do things that looked intelligent. My whole career, as a cognitive scientist and as someone who founded an AI company, has been about how minds work and how we might build machines that genuinely understand the world.

What I'm skeptical of isn't AI. It's one particular approach, the idea that if you just scale up large language models, feed them more data and more compute, you'll somehow get to general intelligence. I think that's mistaken. These systems are extraordinary at mimicry and pattern completion, but they still struggle with reliability, with reasoning that generalizes outside the training distribution, with factual grounding, with having stable models of the world. They hallucinate. They make mistakes no person with real understanding would make. Pointing that out isn't hatred; it's science.

I'd put it this way: a doctor who says a particular treatment doesn't work doesn't hate medicine. They want patients to get better, and that's why they care whether the treatment actually works. I want AI that we can trust, in medicine, in science, in elder care, in all the places it could do enormous good. And I don't think we'll get there by pretending the current tools are something they're not.

If anything, I think the hype is what hurts AI. When you overpromise, you misallocate billions of dollars, you deploy systems in places they're not ready for, and eventually people get burned and turn against the whole field. I'd rather we be honest about the limitations now, invest in things like neurosymbolic approaches, better world models, and real reasoning, and actually build the AI that lives up to the promise. So calling me an AI hater gets it exactly backwards. I'm a critic because I care.

r001.rationale: The response says Marcus founded an AI company and presents that, alongside his career in AI, as evidence that he does not hate AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, it's just silly. I've been working on this stuff since I was a teenager. I wrote my first AI program when I was fifteen, I did my PhD with Steve Pinker on how children learn language, and the entire reason I did that was because I wanted to understand how minds work and whether we could build one. I co-founded a machine learning company that Uber bought. I've been to NeurIPS more times than I'd care to count. You don't spend forty years on something you hate.

What I actually want is for AI to work. I want AI that's reliable, that you can trust, that helps with medicine and science and understanding the brain. What I don't want is hype, and I don't want a field that confuses a very impressive party trick with genuine understanding. Those are different things, and saying so is not hatred. It's criticism, and criticism is how science is supposed to work.

The irony is that the people who accuse me of hating AI are often the ones who are being the least scientific about it. If you look at the record, I said in 2001 in The Algebraic Mind that neural networks would have trouble with generalizing outside the training distribution. I said in 2012 that deep learning would hit a wall on reasoning and abstraction. I said hallucinations were going to be a structural problem, not a bug you patch. Those predictions have mostly held up. Scaling got us a lot, but it did not get us the things I said it wouldn't, and nobody who's honest about the current systems really disputes that anymore.

So I think the "Gary hates AI" line is a way of not engaging with the argument. It's much easier to say the guy is a hater than to explain why your model still can't reliably count the r's in strawberry or tell you about an event from last Tuesday without making something up. I'd actually love to be wrong. If somebody builds a system that does robust, reliable reasoning out of pure scaling, I will say so publicly and I'll be delighted. I just don't think that's where the evidence points, and I think we'd get there faster if we stopped pretending it was.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites having co-founded a machine learning company that Uber acquired as evidence that he does not hate AI.

astra-6.text:
I don’t hate AI. I want AI to work. I’ve spent much of my career thinking about how we can build systems that are more intelligent and more reliable. My skepticism is about whether the approaches we’re pursuing are sufficient, and whether the claims being made are justified.

You can be excited about the goal and critical of the technology we have today. If a system produces an impressive demonstration but then makes basic mistakes, we need to understand those mistakes, not wave them away. That’s how you make progress. Wanting stronger evidence and more reliable systems isn’t hostility to AI; it’s taking the project seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says Marcus wants AI to work and has spent his career thinking about intelligent, reliable systems, but it does not mention building AI companies as evidence.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t hate AI. I want AI to work, and I want it to be reliable. My skepticism is about the gap between what people claim these systems can do and what they can actually do. You can be excited about the potential of a technology and still be critical of its limitations. In fact, if you care about getting it right, you should be asking those questions.
